brief_extract:
FIRST IMPRESSIONS 'DOWN-UNDER'
THE story begins with my flight to New Zealand, where I arrived on September 30th. I left London at 11.30 a.m. on a Monday morning and in 35 hours actual flying time I was in Auckland on Wednesday, having crossed the international date line and flown half round the world.

brief_context: Arrival city and largest city in New Zealand mentioned.
brief_extract: I left London at 11.30 a.m. on a Monday morning and in 35 hours actual flying time I was in Auckland on Wednesday, having crossed the international date line and flown half round the world. The same trip by sea in one of the world's fastest liners still takes 35 days, and it took the first settlers 35 weeks.

location_standardised: Auckland Airport, Mangere, Auckland, New Zealand
brief_context: Place where the author first touched down in New Zealand.
brief_extract: The same trip by sea in one of the world's fastest liners still takes 35 days, and it took the first settlers 35 weeks. These first settlers landed at Auckland—and when I first touched down at Auckland airport I was immediately struck by the fresh green look of the countryside, and this first impression never once left me during the whole time I flew over the country or travelled around. I did, of course, arrive in springtime and everywhere I went this fresh look was enhanced by the beautiful colours of the spring flowers growing both in their natural surroundings and in both public and private gardens.

brief_context: One of the two main islands of New Zealand discussed.
brief_extract: There is not at present any connecting cable between the grid system of the North and South Islands, and the current generated in each island is only therefore available in that island. The generating capacity of the North Island is almost double that of the South Island, but as about two-thirds of New Zealand's total population of 2 1/2 million live in the North Island, mainly in and around Auckland, many people would welcome this connecting link between the two islands. Like many countries in the world today, New Zealand is suffering from a power shortage, and although the natural resources of the country are on her side, it still takes considerable time to build, erect and put into operation new stations.

brief_context: Location where the author observed geo-thermal steam.

Harnessing the steam
I was fortunate during my stay in Auckland to be taken to see for myself the marvels of boiling mud and steaming ground. My first impression upon arriving at Waikerei was that it looked exactly like a steam train standing unseen amongst the hills. As we approached and got nearer, this first impression vanished when I saw great volumes of steam escaping from the bores.

brief_context: One of the countries visited by Vera Stowell.

brief_context: City where Vera Stowell spoke with an elderly chief.
brief_extract:
In the towns
In the towns of Ghana and Nigeria, there is great interest in everything up-to-date and modern. In Lagos I talked with a chief who, having seen some of our equipment and talked about all the modern labour-saving devices, said with feeling, "I never thought I live to see this day". He was elderly, and I thought of the great changes which had taken place in Nigeria during his lifetime.

brief_context: Setting for Nona Baker's wartime experiences.
article_title: PAI NAA The Story of Nona Baker, M.B.E.
brief_extract:
(Constable, 18/-.)
Many E.A.W. members will have heard Miss Baker speak of her life in the Malayan jungle during the war, and will have realised what a world of difference divides the life she led as a white woman with a band of Chinese Communist guerillas fighting the Japanese and her present one as Branch Development Secretary of the E.A.W.! In this graphically told story are some of the details of many months of hardship, and imagination will supply those other details of suspense and tension which must have daily beset Pai Naa who, after her brother had died, did not know that her story would have a happy ending.

brief_extract:
In the last 50 years a tremendous expansion
in vegetable oil production has occurred, in line
with the development of the margarine indus-
try, and millions of farmers throughout the
world now grow the seeds and nuts from which
the oils are produced. These include groundnuts (peanuts) mainly
from Nigeria and India; coconuts from Ceylon,
Malaya, New Guinea, Papua and the British
Pacific Islands; palm oil and palm kernels from
Nigeria and Malaya; cottonseed from the Sudan
and Nigeria; soya beans from China and North
America; and the sunflower known to all gar-
deners but grown commercially in Europe,
China, India and America. Except for palm oil, which must be produced
in the growing area, the oil from these seeds or
nuts can be extracted either in the producing
country or in the importing country.

brief_context: Location where Hopkins discovered vitamins.
brief_extract:
Modern research
Margarine research over the last few decades
has been concentrated, first, on the nutritional
content of the food, and second, on flavour and
texture. In 1912 Sir Frederick Gowland Hop-
kins discovered at Cambridge that foodstuffs
contained minute amounts of unsuspected sub-
stances that are now known as vitamins. In the
early days it was believed that certain oils and
fats contained a single vitamin—known at first
as Fat-Soluble A—which experiments in the
diets of rats proved to be essential to normal
growth, the ordinary calcification of the bone,
and the prevention both of rickets and of an eye
disease.

location_standardised: King's Lynn, Norfolk, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: The historic port town described in the article.
brief_extract:
HANCOCK, Magazine Secretary, King’s Lynn Branch
Once the third port in the kingdom,
King’s Lynn is full of treasures of a historic past,
which are enhanced by electricity. At the same time
this ‘treasure’ of the modern era provides comfort
and prosperity to the citizens of to-day
The 17th century Customs House
IF you are visiting East Anglia and pass through the attractive old town of King's Lynn on the way to see the Royal residence at Sandringham or having a holiday on the famous Broads, then you should certainly pause a while and take a look at the treasures of a more leisurely age with which this town is blessed. This town has a history by accident; from a few homesteads on a mud flat, hardly mentioned in Domesday Book, it rose to become the third port in the country after what was probably a 12th century tidal surge, similar to the one that hit the East Coast in 1953, but this one changed the course of the River Ouse which at that time entered the Wash at Wisbech and brought it to King's Lynn.

brief_context: Source of whales for lamp oil in an earlier age.
brief_extract: There is also an almost complete set of Council Minutes from 1431. So far I have told you of the gems of an earlier age, an age when many of the populace used lamps in their homes fed with the oil of whales caught in the North Sea, landed in the port and the oil extracted in the town; there was, up to recent times, a watercourse in the town known locally as Blubber Creek. Then in 1898 the Corporation decided to enter a new historical phase and erected a small direct current power house; the electrical age had come to an ancient borough, and the generators still supply a very small part of the town, but very soon the complete change to alternating current from the national grid will be made.

location_standardised: The Wash, Norfolk, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Area where King John is said to have lost jewels.
brief_extract:
Here is buried Robinson Crusoe, Daniel Defoe visited Lynn about the time he wrote the story of Alexander Selkirk, and quite possibly met this Robinson Crusoe and used his name as a pseudonym. The Borough is proud of its municipal treasures among which is the wonderful and priceless early 14th century silver gilt and enamel loving cup known as the King John Cup —nothing to do with the King who lost his jewels in the Wash, though he did present the
two-handed sword to the Mayor of the time and this is still carried before the Mayor in civic ceremony; there are also the silver wine beakers and an early set of salt cellars. Then again the visitors will be shown a fine set of charters presented to the borough by different kings, the earliest being the one presented by King John in 1204, a manuscript from the time of King Canute, and the famous Red Register commenced in 1307, which is one of the earliest of paper books.
